subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan after a bad mock score [Revision]
passage: “Hemant, you're my best friend, so you get the whole story. I'm Dilnaz, and my third mock dropped by thirty marks. My first reaction was to panic and blame the paper. Then I made myself look. My sleep log said five hours a night all week. My mistakes were mostly in electrostatics. So I changed two things. I dropped Sunday cricket for two weeks, and I added twenty short physics problems every evening. I'm also writing my mock score, sleep hours and mood on one page each Saturday. Honestly, I don't know yet if it's working. I'll compare the next two mocks and decide from that, not from how I feel.”

qa.q: What did Dilnaz drop for two weeks?
What did Dilnaz feel when the third mock dropped?
qa.a: Panic at first, then a calmer wish to find the causes instead of blaming the paper.

qa.q: What else could Dilnaz do if scores do not recover, and why?
qa.a: Ask a teacher to look over the mistakes, since fresh eyes may find gaps that self-checking misses.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Dilnaz's change?
qa.a: Hemant sees a friend who dealt with a bad result methodically rather than blaming luck, and may feel reassured or want to try a similar log.

grounding: After a drop in a mock, a student checks sleep and topic gaps, cuts an activity, adds daily problems and tracks recovery.
